# Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?

Jeonghye Kim, Xufang Luo, Minbeom Kim, Sangmook Lee, Dohyung Kim, Jiwon
Jeon, Dongsheng Li, Yuqing Yang Microsoft Research  KAIST  SK hynix 
Seoul National University ![[Uncaptioned
image]](2603.24472v4/figure/logo/link.png)  [blog
post](https://beanie00.notion.site/why-does-self-distillation-degrade-reasoning?source=copy_link)

  

 
[beanie00/self-distillation-analysis](https://github.com/beanie00/self-distillation-analysis)

###### Abstract

Self-distillation has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for
LLMs, often improving performance while shortening reasoning traces.
However, in mathematical reasoning, we find that it can reduce response
length while degrading performance. We trace this degradation to the
suppression of epistemic verbalization—the model’s expression of
uncertainty during reasoning. Through controlled experiments varying
conditioning context richness and task coverage, we show that
conditioning the teacher on rich information suppresses uncertainty
expression, enabling rapid in-domain optimization with limited task
coverage but harming OOD performance, where unseen problems benefit from
expressing uncertainty and adjusting accordingly. Across Qwen3-1.7B/8B,
DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B, and Olmo3-7B-Instruct, we observe performance
drops of up to 40%. Our findings highlight that exposing appropriate
levels of uncertainty is crucial for robust reasoning and underscore the
importance of optimizing reasoning behavior beyond merely reinforcing
correct answer traces.

| --- |
|     |

## 1 Introduction

(a) Chemistry (Olmo3-7B-Instruct)

(b) DAPO-Math-17k (DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B)

Figure 1: (a) Training score and response length changes for GRPO and
Self-Distillation (SDPO) ([Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) in
Chemistry, using results from SDPO Wandb logs ([Biewald,
2020](#bib.bib8)) [(link)](https://wandb.ai/jonhue/SDPO?nw=mgotcx6kk7).
(b) Training score and response length changes on DAPO-Math-17k with
GRPO and SDPO.

Recently, self-distillation ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib7)) has
attracted increasing attention in the post-training of large language
models (LLMs). In this paradigm, two instances of the same model are
employed: one conditioned on privileged information (e.g., ground-truth
solutions) serves as a teacher, providing dense reward signals for
responses generated by another instance that does not have access to
that information. Several studies have demonstrated that combining this
framework with post-training methods such as Reinforcement Learning from
Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) leads to highly efficient performance gains
([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib9); [Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib2);
[Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Penaloza et al., 2026](#bib.bib20);
[Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib1); [Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)). These
methods have shown particularly strong improvements in domains such as
agentic environments and scientific reasoning, especially under
in-domain evaluation settings. Interestingly, a consistent trend
observed across these works is that performance improves as response
length decreases, suggesting that self-distillation promotes more
concise and effective reasoning.

However, when we apply the same self-distillation approach to
mathematical reasoning tasks, we observe a markedly different
phenomenon.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
compares the effects of a representative self-distillation algorithm,
SDPO, in the Chemistry domain (a) and the Math domain (b). As shown in
the figure, in the Chemistry domain, self-distillation substantially
reduces response length compared to GRPO while rapidly improving
performance. In contrast, in the Math domain, although response length
consistently decreases as training progresses, performance drops
significantly, contrary to prior findings.

This raises a question: _”Why does performance sometimes degrade despite
the model being trained to move toward the correct answer?”_

Our analysis reveals a consistent pattern: the more informative the
context provided to the teacher, the more concise and confident the
resulting reasoning becomes, with substantially fewer expressions of
uncertainty and, particularly in math reasoning, degraded performance.
We trace this effect to the suppression of epistemic verbalization ([Kim
et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)), whereby models explicitly verbalize and
incorporate uncertainty during reasoning. Strong reasoning models such
as DeepSeek-R1 ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)) frequently express
uncertainty using tokens like “Wait” or “Hmm”. Although these
expressions may not directly advance the reasoning, removing them
discards important signals that a reasoning path may be flawed, leading
to significant performance drops ([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)).

To systematically understand when and why self-distillation suppresses
epistemic verbalization and thus affects performance, we conduct a
comprehensive empirical study and identify two key factors: information
richness and task coverage. The more privileged the information the
teacher receives, such as the correct solution, the more its reasoning
traces suppress expressions of uncertainty, encouraging the student to
imitate a confident reasoning style that presupposes information
unavailable at inference time. When task coverage is limited, this
compression enables rapid in-domain optimization. However, as coverage
increases, removing epistemic verbalization can interfere with
optimization across diverse tasks, degrading performance on more
challenging or unseen problems.

More broadly, our results show that even when the training objective
faithfully guides the model toward correct reasoning traces, the
resulting reasoning style can quietly shift in ways that hurt
generalization. The suppression of epistemic verbalization is not
penalized by standard objectives, yet negatively impacts
out-of-distribution (OOD) performance. This suggests that post-training
objectives need to account not only for answer correctness, but also for
eliciting and preserving uncertainty-aware reasoning behaviors. We
believe these findings offer a useful step toward a deeper understanding
of reasoning in self-distillation and post-training more broadly.

## 2 Preliminaries

#### Self-Distillation

Let $`x\in\mathcal{X}`$ denote an input and $`y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T})`$ a
sequence generated by a language model $`\pi_{\theta}`$. The model
defines an autoregressive distribution
$`\pi_{\theta}(y|x)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}).`$
In self-distillation, the same model acts as both a _student_ and a
_teacher_ under different conditioning contexts. The student first
generates a sequence $`y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$. The teacher
policy is obtained by conditioning the model on a _richer context_ $`c`$
that provides additional information about the input (e.g., solutions,
environment feedback, or other auxiliary signals). Training minimizes
the divergence between the student and teacher next-token distributions:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{\text{Self-Distillation}}}(\theta)=\sum_{t}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\;\|\;\mathrm{stopgrad}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,c,y_{<t})\big)\right).
``` |  | (1) |

This objective encourages the student to match the teacher’s predictions
under the richer context, enabling the model to improve by distilling
privileged information available at training time without requiring an
external teacher.

#### Key Characteristics of Math Reasoning

In LLMs, math reasoning can be viewed as self-Bayesian reasoning, where
each step is generated conditioned only on the prompt $`x`$ and
previously generated tokens $`y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T})`$, allowing the
model to iteratively update its belief over intermediate hypotheses
([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). Such reasoning spans diverse tasks such
as arithmetic, algebra, geometry, word problems, and logical pattern
recognition, so evaluation benchmarks are frequently OOD relative to
training data due to compositional and reasoning-depth shifts.

![Refer to
caption](2603.24472v4/figure/sec2/Reasoning_with_Epistemic_Verbalization.png)

(2a) Reasoning with Epistemic Verbalization

![Refer to
caption](2603.24472v4/figure/sec2/unguided_vs_teacher_guided.png)

(2b) Unguided vs. Solution-Guided

Within this process, verbalized uncertainty toward correct response
$`y^{*}`$, referred to as epistemic verbalization ([Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6)), can serve as an informative signal rather than
stylistic redundancy. As shown in
Figure [2(2a)](#S2.F2.sf1 "In Key Characteristics of Math Reasoning ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
reasoning without such signals may prematurely commit to incorrect
hypotheses with little room for recovery, whereas epistemic
verbalization preserves alternative hypotheses and supports gradual
uncertainty reduction.

## 3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information

In self-distillation, the teacher has access to a richer context $`c`$,
which provides strong hints and enables it to generate reasoning traces
with minimal expressed uncertainty (Figure
[2(2b)](#S2.F2.sf2 "In Key Characteristics of Math Reasoning ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")).
While this yields more concise responses, it could eliminate not only
unnecessary verbosity but also valuable epistemic signals, potentially
hindering the student’s ability to perform uncertainty-aware reasoning.
This raises two questions we investigate: (i) how does the richness of
$`c`$ relate to the suppression of uncertainty expression and to
reasoning performance? and (ii) if epistemic verbalization is
beneficial, why does suppressing it improve performance in domains such
as Chemistry while degrading it in Math?

To study these questions, we first need a way to quantify how
informative the conditioning context is. Let $`y^{*}`$ denote a random
variable representing an ideal correct response to $`x`$. We formalize
the information that $`c`$ provides about $`y^{*}`$ as the conditional
mutual information

|     |                                                               |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       I(y^{*};\,c\mid x)\;=\;H(y^{*}\mid x)\;-\;H(y^{*}\mid x,\,c),
       ```                                                            |     | (2) |

which captures the reduction in uncertainty about $`y^{*}`$ once the
additional context $`c`$ is given.

Building on this measure, we construct a controlled comparison to
examine how the model’s reasoning behavior changes as the conditioning
information is varied. We use the DAPO-Math-17k dataset ([Yu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4)) with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)) as the base model, selecting 100 problems on which
the base model achieves accuracy between 0.125 and 0.5 over 8 rollouts.
Let $`s`$ denote the full solution (including chain-of-thought in
\<think\> tags), $`s_{\setminus\text{think}}`$ the solution with
\<think\> content removed, and $`y_{r}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,s)`$
a response previously generated under full solution guidance. We compare
the model’s responses across four generation settings:

- •
  (1) Unguided generation ($`c=\emptyset`$): $`I(y^{*};\,c\mid x)=0`$ by
  definition.
- •
  (2) Solution-guided generation ($`c=s`$): provides maximal guidance
  and yields the largest $`I(y^{*};\,c\mid x)`$.
- •
  (3) Solution-guided generation without think contents
  ($`c=s_{\setminus\text{think}}`$): since $`s_{\setminus\text{think}}`$
  is a strict informational subset of $`s`$, we have
  $`I(y^{*};\,s_{\setminus\text{think}}\mid x)\leq I(y^{*};\,s\mid x)`$.
- •
  (4) Regeneration-conditioned generation ($`c=y_{r}`$, where
  $`y_{r}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,s)`$): since $`y_{r}`$ is derived
  from $`s`$, the data processing inequality gives
  $`I(y^{*};\,y_{r}\mid x)\leq I(y^{*};\,s\mid x)`$.

These settings induce the following ordering over the conditional mutual
information:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\underbrace{I(y^{*};\,\emptyset\mid x)=0}_{\text{(1)}}\;<\;\underbrace{I(y^{*};\,s_{\setminus\text{think}}\mid x)}_{\text{(3)}}\;\leq\;\underbrace{I(y^{*};\,y_{r}\mid x)}_{\text{(4)}}\;\leq\;\underbrace{I(y^{*};\,s\mid x)}_{\text{(2)}}.
``` |  | (3) |

#### Prompts

The prompts used for unguided and solution-guided settings are as
follows. For regeneration, we used the same prompts as in [Hübotter et
al. (2026)](#bib.bib2). A comparative analysis with other regeneration
prompts is provided in Appendix
[H](#A8 "Appendix H Can Uncertainty-Encouraging Prompts Mitigate the Suppression? ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").

[TABLE]

#### Epistemic Tokens

Following [Kim et al. (2026)](#bib.bib6), we define a set of 10
epistemic markers
$`\mathcal{T}=\{\textit{wait},\,\textit{hmm},\,\textit{perhaps},\,\textit{maybe},\,\textit{actually},\,\textit{alternatively},\,\textit{seems},\,\textit{might},\,\textit{likely},\,\textit{check}\}`$
as practical indicators of regions where the externalization of
uncertainty is likely to occur. These tokens are intuitively
recognizable as uncertainty expressions, with their selection further
supported by a cross-family analysis of 9,600 reasoning traces
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Basis for Selecting Epistemic Tokens ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")).
We measure the epistemic token count of a response $`y`$ as
$`E(y)=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathrm{count}(t,\,y)`$.

#### Results

We analyze how different forms of conditioning information toward the
correct answer affect the model’s reasoning behavior by comparing the
average response length $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$, score, and the epistemic
token count $`\mathbb{E}[E(y)]`$ across the four settings. As shown in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Results ‣ 3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
both quantities decrease monotonically as $`I(y^{*};\,c\mid x)`$
increases:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\bigl[L(y)\bigr]\Big|_{(1)}\;>\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[L(y)\bigr]\Big|_{(3)}\;>\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[L(y)\bigr]\Big|_{(4)}\;>\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[L(y)\bigr]\Big|_{(2)},
``` |  | (4) |

and analogously for $`\mathbb{E}[E(y)]`$, confirming that richer
conditioning information leads to more concise and confident reasoning.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  Avg. Score |  Avg. Length |  Epistemic Token Count |
|  (1) Unguided |  0.30 |  13,054 |  182.5 |
|  (2) Solution-Guided ($`c=s`$) |  0.98 |  1,873 |  8.8 |
|  (3) Solution-Guided ($`c=s_{\setminus\text{think}}`$) |  0.78 |  12,036 |  159.8 |
|  (4) Regeneration-Conditioned |  0.95 |  2,808 |  24.1 |

Table 1: Comparison of response characteristics under varying levels of
rich information.

Specifically, unguided generation ($`c=\emptyset`$) produces
substantially longer responses with the highest epistemic token counts.
When the full solution $`s`$ is provided in (2), the model follows the
given reasoning trace with high confidence, and its concise output can
be viewed as a compressed representation of the reasoning in $`s`$.
In (3), removing the \<think\> portion retains only
$`s_{\setminus\text{think}}`$ (640 out of 13,054 response tokens), and
both $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$ and $`\mathbb{E}[E(y)]`$ increase again toward
the unguided level, reflecting the substantial information loss.
Setting (4), conditioning on the regenerated response $`y_{r}`$, yields
intermediate values (lower than (3) but higher than (2)), indicating
that $`y_{r}`$ preserves much of the informative structure of the full
solution. Detailed per-token breakdowns are reported in
Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Per-Token Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").

## 4 Supervised Finetuning with Self-Distillation

A natural follow-up question is whether the suppression of epistemic
verbalization under high $`I(y^{*};\,c\mid x)`$ is merely stylistic or
has a tangible impact on reasoning capability. To test this, we conduct
off-policy self-distillation (SFT) using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B
([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)) on two datasets, each containing 800
correct responses:

- •
  $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{ug}}`$: unguided responses ($`c=\emptyset`$),
  with high $`\mathbb{E}[E(y)]`$ and
  $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]\approx 12\text{k}`$ tokens.
- •
  $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{sg}}`$: solution-guided responses ($`c=s`$), with
  low $`\mathbb{E}[E(y)]`$ and $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]\approx 2\text{k}`$
  tokens.

Both datasets consist entirely of correct trajectories. The key
difference lies in the epistemic density of the training signal. We
evaluate the resulting checkpoints across multiple math benchmarks
(examples from each dataset are presented in
Appendix [K.1](#A11.SS1 "K.1 Unguided vs. Solution-Guided Generation ‣ Appendix K Qualitative Analysis ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")).

|                                      |          |          |         |           |
|--------------------------------------|----------|----------|---------|-----------|
|  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B         |  AIME24  |  AIME25  |  AMC23  |  MATH500  |
|  Base                                |  54.79   |  37.92   |  89.06  |  92.19    |
|  SFT on $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{ug}}`$  |  51.04   |  40.00   |  87.66  |  90.93    |
|  SFT on $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{sg}}`$  |  20.21   |  12.71   |  57.03  |  65.52    |

Table 2: Math benchmark performance of the base model
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and its SFT checkpoints trained on unguided
and solution-guided datasets.

As shown in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Supervised Finetuning with Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
training on $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{sg}}`$ leads to substantial degradation
across all benchmarks, despite the dataset consisting of correct
answers, whereas training on $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{ug}}`$ produces no
significant performance change. This asymmetry arises because
solution-guided responses are concise precisely due to the external
context $`s`$. Using them as SFT targets forces the model to imitate a
reasoning style that presupposes information unavailable at inference
time, effectively suppressing the epistemic tokens that support
autonomous exploration and error correction.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation

We now turn to on-policy self-distillation ([Hübotter et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2); [Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Penaloza et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20)), where the model learns from dense reward signals
provided by a self-teacher with access to the correct solution, based on
its own responses. We compare GRPO with Reinforcement Learning via
Self-Distillation (SDPO) ([Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) on the
DAPO-Math-17k dataset ([Yu et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)), using Qwen3-8B
([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B ([Guo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). Additional results for Qwen3-1.7B and
Olmo-3-7B-Instruct ([Olmo et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)) are in Appendix
[J.3](#A10.SS3 "J.3 Olmo-3-7B-Instruct ‣ Appendix J More On-Policy Self-Distillation Results ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").
For each model, we track training score, response length, and OOD
performance on AIME24 and AMC23. We fix the teacher to the initial
policy, which performs better than a moving target (see
Section [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Ablation Study: Fixed vs. Moving Target Teacher ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
for a comparison).

The behavior of on-policy self-distillation depends on two factors: (i)
the extent of epistemic verbalization already present in the base model,
and (ii) the richness of the conditioning context $`c`$. To disentangle
these, we compare GRPO and SDPO under two settings: $`c=s`$ (full
solution) and $`c=s_{\setminus\text{think}}`$ (solution without
\<think\> content).

### 5.1 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B

a Training Score-Length Comparison

b AMC23 Score and Response Length

c AIME24 Score and Response Length

d Change in Epistemic Token Usage on AIME24

Figure 3: On-policy self-distillation results for
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. GRPO yields modest OOD gains with a slight
increase in epistemic verbalization, whereas SDPO degrades both
performance and epistemic token usage, particularly with $`c=s`$.

DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is a representative high-reasoning model
that generates rich epistemic verbalizations within \<think\> tags,
averaging about 180 epistemic tokens per response, as shown in
Section [3](#S3 "3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
leading to lengthy yet high-performing reasoning outputs.

#### Training Performance

As shown in
Figure [3a](#S5.F3.sf1 "In Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
GRPO training slightly increases $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$ with a modest
improvement in score. In contrast, SDPO with $`c=s`$ causes a sharp
initial drop in both $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$ and score. Performance
gradually recovers but remains below GRPO throughout training. When the
conditioning is reduced to $`c=s_{\setminus\text{think}}`$, the drop in
$`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$ is attenuated and the score trajectory approaches
that of GRPO, consistent with the relationship between
$`I(y^{*};\,c\mid x)`$ and epistemic suppression discussed in
Section [3](#S3 "3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").

#### OOD Evaluation - AIME24, AMC23

Consistent with the training trends, GRPO yields modest gains on both
OOD benchmarks (AIME24: 54.7 $`\to`$ 56.0; AMC23: 89.3 $`\to`$ 91.1,
Figures
[3b](#S5.F3.sf2 "In Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
and
[3c](#S5.F3.sf3 "In Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"))
with a slight increase in $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$. SDPO with $`c=s`$
degrades performance substantially ($`{\sim}40\%`$ on AIME24,
$`{\sim}15\%`$ on AMC23). Reducing the conditioning to
$`c=s_{\setminus\text{think}}`$ mitigates the drop, though performance
still remains below the base model.

#### Reasoning Pattern

Figure [3d](#S5.F3.sf4 "In Figure 3 ‣ 5.1 DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
illustrates the epistemic token counts of the trained models. GRPO
increases $`\mathbb{E}[E(y)]`$, whereas SDPO suppresses it more
aggressively, consistent with the observed correlation between epistemic
suppression and performance degradation throughout our analysis.
Additional analyses on total versus epistemic token changes, as well as
the number of uncertainty expressions per reasoning trace, evaluated
using an LLM-as-Judge, are provided in
Appendices [E.4](#A5.SS4 "E.4 Comparative Analysis of Epistemic and Overall Word Usage ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
and
[E.5](#A5.SS5 "E.5 Uncertainty Annotation via LLM-as-Judge ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").
Furthermore, a comparison of the KL divergence of epistemic tokens with
respect to the mean is presented in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Student–Teacher KL Divergence on Epistemic Tokens ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").
Example responses generated by GRPO and SDPO are included in
Appendix [K.2](#A11.SS2 "K.2 GRPO vs. SDPO Generation ‣ Appendix K Qualitative Analysis ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").

### 5.2 Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: ON)

Qwen3-8B is a hybrid reasoning model that can operate in either a
thinking mode for deliberate reasoning or a non-thinking mode for direct
responses. With thinking mode enabled, Qwen3-8B produces longer
responses than DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, with a higher number of
epistemic tokens (see
Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Comparison of Epistemic Token Usage Across Models ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
for a comparison of epistemic tokens across models).

a Training Score-Length Comparison

b AMC23 Score and Response Length

c AIME24 Score and Response Length

d Change in Epistemic Token Usage on AIME24

Figure 4: On-policy self-distillation results for Qwen3-8B (Thinking
Mode: ON). Both GRPO and SDPO reduce response length and epistemic
verbalization, but SDPO’s more aggressive suppression leads to greater
degradation in OOD performance, particularly on AIME24.

#### Training Performance

As shown in
Figure [4a](#S5.F4.sf1 "In Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: ON) ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
$`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$ decreases under both GRPO and SDPO, with SDPO
exhibiting a larger reduction and a correspondingly larger performance
drop. Notably, $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$ first drops sharply, then increases
slightly. Since the teacher policy is fixed as the reference policy,
shortening the response by $`{\sim}900`$ tokens reduces the
informativeness of $`c`$, i.e., decreases $`I(y^{*},c\mid x)`$. As the
context becomes less informative, the model compensates by increasing
epistemic verbalization, causing the length to partially recover.

#### OOD Evaluation - AIME24, AMC23

The gap becomes more pronounced on OOD benchmarks
(Figures [4b](#S5.F4.sf2 "In Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: ON) ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
and
[4c](#S5.F4.sf3 "In Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: ON) ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")):
GRPO maintains largely stable performance with gradually decreasing
$`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$, whereas SDPO falls below the base model,
particularly with $`c=s`$. Notably, although GRPO and SDPO with
$`c=s_{\setminus\text{think}}`$ achieve comparable training performance,
their OOD results diverge, especially on the more challenging AIME24,
where SDPO with $`c=s_{\setminus\text{think}}`$ shows progressive
performance degradation as training proceeds.

#### Reasoning Pattern

Figure [4d](#S5.F4.sf4 "In Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: ON) ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
reveals that both methods reduce $`\mathbb{E}[E(y)]`$ relative to the
base model, with SDPO more aggressively so. This suggests that Qwen3-8B
originally generates more epistemic verbalization than necessary. While
both methods mitigate this redundancy, overly aggressive suppression
risks removing epistemic signals that carry useful reasoning
information.

### 5.3 Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: OFF)

a Training Score-Length Comparison

b AIME24 Score and Response Length

Figure 5: On-policy self-distillation results for Qwen3-8B (Thinking
Mode: OFF). GRPO rapidly increases response length via epistemic
verbalization and achieves strong training gains, while SDPO reduces
response length and struggles to improve, with slight OOD degradation on
AIME24.

When Qwen3-8B is used without thinking mode, the \<think\> tag is
absent, so we consider only $`c=s`$. The model initially produces much
shorter responses and exhibits significantly lower performance. GRPO
rapidly increases $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$ by promoting epistemic
verbalization (as shown in
Appendix [J.1](#A10.SS1 "J.1 Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: OFF) ‣ Appendix J More On-Policy Self-Distillation Results ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")),
quickly achieving a high training score. In contrast, SDPO reduces
$`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$ and improves much more slowly. Even when the
training score slightly increases, as shown in
Figure [5b](#S5.F5.sf2 "In Figure 5 ‣ 5.3 Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: OFF) ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
performance on AIME24 slightly declines ($`0.25\to 0.23`$), further
illustrating the cost of epistemic suppression under self-distillation.

### 5.4 Causal Study: Epistemic Token Suppression during GRPO

To further examine whether the suppression of epistemic verbalization is
a causal contributor to the observed performance degradation, we
explicitly penalized epistemic tokens during GRPO training and tested
whether this intervention induces a similar degradation pattern.

Following the epistemic marker set $`\mathcal{T}`$ defined in
Section [3](#S3 "3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
we override the standard GRPO advantage at every position $`t`$ whose
generated token realizes a marker in $`\mathcal{T}`$, setting
$`\tilde{A}_{t}=\min(A_{t},-\kappa)`$ if $`y_{t}\in\mathcal{T}`$ and
$`\tilde{A}_{t}=A_{t}`$ otherwise, with suppression strength
$`\kappa=0.5`$. Since $`\tilde{A}_{t}\leq-\kappa`$ holds even for
correct rollouts, the policy gradient consistently reduces
$`\mathbb{E}[E(y)]`$ throughout training.

a DeepSeek-Distill-7B Training Comparison

b DeepSeek-Distill-7B AIME24 Comparison

Figure 6: Effect of epistemic-token suppression during GRPO for
DeepSeek-Distill-7B.

As shown in
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.4 Causal Study: Epistemic Token Suppression during GRPO ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
explicitly penalizing epistemic tokens during GRPO produces shorter
responses and lower performance, qualitatively reproducing the
degradation pattern observed with SDPO. The degradation is less
pronounced than under SDPO, possibly because the predefined epistemic
token set does not capture all linguistic realizations of uncertainty or
epistemic reasoning, as discussed further in
Appendix [E.5](#A5.SS5 "E.5 Uncertainty Annotation via LLM-as-Judge ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").
Nevertheless, this result provides causal evidence that suppressing
uncertainty expression contributes to the performance decline under
SDPO.

### 5.5 Ablation Study: Fixed vs. Moving Target Teacher

In naive on-policy self-distillation, the teacher and student share a
continuously updated policy, making the teacher a moving target that can
introduce training instability ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Ye et
al., 2026](#bib.bib5)). To mitigate this, SDPO uses an EMA-smoothed
teacher (EMA rate: 0.05). However, we find that setting the EMA rate to
0.0 (i.e., fixing the teacher to the initial policy) yields better
performance, and thus
Section [5](#S5 "5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
follows this setting.

a DeepSeek-Distill-7B Training Comparison

b DeepSeek-Distill-7B AIME24 Comparison

Figure 7: Fixed vs. moving target teacher for
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Even slow EMA updates (rate 0.05) amplify
epistemic suppression via a feedback loop, causing greater performance
degradation than a fixed teacher.

Figure [7a](#S5.F7.sf1 "In Figure 7 ‣ 5.5 Ablation Study: Fixed vs. Moving Target Teacher ‣ 5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
shows additional comparison results when the teacher is updated during
training. As shown, even slow updates (e.g., rate 0.05) lead to a
sharper reduction in response length, resulting in larger performance
degradation. This can be interpreted as a feedback loop in
self-distillation. The model is trained to produce increasingly
confident outputs, and when this is used as the teacher, it generates
even more confident responses, amplifying the effect over iterations.
Further ablations on learning rate, top-$`k`$ logits, and the effect of
limiting the maximum response length to 4,096 tokens are provided in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D More Ablation Study ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").

## 6 Relationship Between Task Coverage, Epistemic Verbalization and Generalization Ability

Across the off-policy and on-policy settings analyzed above,
self-distillation consistently produces more confident responses with
reduced $`\mathbb{E}[E(y)]`$. This aligns with the findings of [Hübotter
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2), which reports that SDPO learns to reason
concisely: on Science Q&A (Chemistry, Physics, Biology, and Materials
Science) ([Feng et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)), tool use ([Tang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib14)), and LiveCodeBench v6 ([Jain et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15)), SDPO achieves higher accuracy than GRPO while
producing substantially shorter outputs with fewer epistemic markers.

In other words, in these domains, self-distillation suppresses epistemic
verbalization and improves performance simultaneously. The key question
is *why the same mechanism leads to performance degradation in our
math-focused setup*. We hypothesize that the answer lies in differences
in task coverage between the training and evaluation distributions.

### 6.1 Comparison of Task Coverage

To test this hypothesis, we compare the dataset characteristics of the
settings where SDPO outperformed GRPO against our experimental setup. As
shown in
Table [3](#S6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 6.1 Comparison of Task Coverage ‣ 6 Relationship Between Task Coverage, Epistemic Verbalization and Generalization Ability ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
the Chemistry dataset, despite its large size, draws from only six main
problem types that differ primarily in surface details rather than
underlying structure. LiveCodeBench v6 contains diverse problems but
only 131 in total, leading to repeated exposure during training with
identical train/eval splits. In contrast, DAPO-Math-17k exposes the
model to  14,000 distinct problems (78% of the 25,600 samples drawn over
100 steps, due to repeated sampling), spanning a broad, non-overlapping
range of problem types, and evaluation is performed on unseen problem
types.

[TABLE]

Table 3: Comparison of the total number of problems, problem
composition, and train–evaluation splits in ScienceQ&A, LiveCodeBench
v6, and our experiments.

### 6.2 Relationship Between Task Coverage and Learning Performance

To further investigate the interplay between task coverage and
generalization, we vary the number of training questions
$`|\mathcal{D}|\in\{1,8,64,128,512\}`$ from DAPO-Math-17k and train with
both GRPO and SDPO. All experiments use Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode OFF).

#### Training Logs

As shown in Figure
[8](#S6.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Training Logs ‣ 6.2 Relationship Between Task Coverage and Learning Performance ‣ 6 Relationship Between Task Coverage, Epistemic Verbalization and Generalization Ability ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
GRPO and SDPO exhibit distinct training dynamics as $`|\mathcal{D}|`$
varies. When $`|\mathcal{D}|\leq 128`$, SDPO quickly achieves high
scores while reducing $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$ by up to $`8\times`$,
indicating higher training efficiency on a small task set. However, at
$`|\mathcal{D}|=512`$, further reductions in $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$ begin
to hurt the training score relative to GRPO, whose $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$
gradually increases with $`|\mathcal{D}|`$.

Figure 8: Training score and response length comparison between GRPO and
SDPO for $`|D|\in\{1,8,64,128,512\}`$.

This difference can be interpreted through task coverage. As
$`|\mathcal{D}|`$ grows, the model must accommodate a broader range of
reasoning patterns. GRPO addresses this by increasing
$`\mathbb{E}[E(y)]`$, allowing the model to express greater uncertainty
and adapt its reasoning accordingly. SDPO instead encourages confident,
concise responses—effective when task coverage is small but limiting
when the problem set becomes larger and more diverse.

Figure 9: Evaluation performance on AIME24 and MATH500 and response
length as $`|D|`$ varies over {1, 8, 64, 128, 512}.

#### OOD Evaluation - AIME24, MATH500

The distinction between GRPO and SDPO becomes more pronounced on OOD
benchmarks
(Figure [9](#S6.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Training Logs ‣ 6.2 Relationship Between Task Coverage and Learning Performance ‣ 6 Relationship Between Task Coverage, Epistemic Verbalization and Generalization Ability ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")).
Under GRPO, performance scales consistently with $`|\mathcal{D}|`$:
$`|\mathcal{D}|=1`$ converges quickly but soon stops improving, while
larger $`|\mathcal{D}|`$ yields progressively higher final scores
accompanied by increasing $`\mathbb{E}[L(y)]`$. Under SDPO, the pattern
reverses: smaller $`|\mathcal{D}|`$ leads to more severe OOD
degradation. Even at the largest $`|\mathcal{D}|`$ (DAPO setting), SDPO
still underperforms the base model. Changes in GRPO and SDPO reasoning
patterns across task coverage are provided in
Appendix [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Analysis of GRPO and SDPO Reasoning Patterns by Task Coverage ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 7 Conclusion

In this work, we provide an empirical analysis of on-policy
self-distillation, motivated by an information-theoretic view of
conditioning context richness. Our experiments suggest that the
effectiveness of self-distillation is closely tied to how information is
provided to the model and how the model expresses uncertainty during
reasoning. We observe that self-distillation tends to produce answers
with higher confidence and shorter reasoning traces. While this effect
enables more compact reasoning and can quickly improve in-domain
performance when task coverage is limited, it becomes less effective
when task coverage is broad and may even harm OOD performance.

Importantly, the fact that performance can degrade even when a
mathematically sound objective function is designed to elicit correct
CoT reasoning suggests that the choice of optimization objective alone
may not be sufficient for preserving robust reasoning, and that we need
to pay closer attention to how training reshapes the model’s reasoning
behavior, beyond answer correctness. We hope that our analysis
contributes to a deeper understanding of self-distillation and other LLM
post-training methods, and provides insights for developing more robust
training strategies.

## Ethics Statement

This work aims to analyze the causes of reasoning performance
degradation during self-distillation of LLMs. All experiments were
conducted using publicly available models (Qwen3,
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen, OLMo) and datasets (DAPO-Math-17k, AIME, AMC,
MATH500). As this study does not involve any new data collection or
human subjects research, concerns related to privacy or human subjects
ethics do not apply.

A key finding of this work is that self-distillation can suppress
epistemic verbalization, thereby diminishing a model’s ability to
express uncertainty during reasoning. This observation carries important
implications for the design of LLM post-training methods. The ability to
appropriately express uncertainty is directly related to model
reliability and safety. Training procedures that indiscriminately
suppress such expressions may increase the risk of models producing
incorrect answers with unwarranted confidence. We hope that our analysis
contributes to the development of more robust and trustworthy reasoning
models.

## Reproducibility Statement

We release our implementation and experiment scripts at [GitHub
(beanie00/self-distillation-analysis)](https://github.com/beanie00/self-distillation-analysis),
along with our training logs on [Weights &
Biases](https://wandb.ai/beanie/SDPO-beanie/reports/Why-Does-Self-Distillation-Sometimes-Degrade-the-Reasoning-Capability-of-LLMs---VmlldzoxNjI1MTk5Mw?accessToken=i1ohtk0lbrcm63kkv1vd99f6jvb71sqoj32rgsokrs4l8r4vjz8q5mywtt8upwho),
and trained checkpoints for the main model settings on [Hugging Face
(beanie00/self-distillation-analysis)](https://huggingface.co/collections/beanie00/self-distillation-analysis).

The repository provides instructions and scripts for data preparation,
GRPO/SDPO training, task-coverage experiments, and evaluation. Detailed
prompts, training hyperparameters, and evaluation configurations are
provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").

## Appendix A Related Works

#### Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning.

Self-distillation, where a single model acts as both teacher and student
under asymmetric conditioning ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib7)), has
recently been widely adopted for LLM post-training. SDPO ([Hübotter et
al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) conditions the self-teacher on its previously
generated correct trajectories or rich environment feedback to provide
dense credit assignment, while OPSD ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib3))
leverages ground-truth solutions as privileged information, achieving
strong efficiency gains in both cases. Our analysis builds upon the SDPO
codebase, and a detailed comparison with OPSD is provided in
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Comparison with OPSD from ( ) ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").
[Liu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib1); [Penaloza et al. (2026)](#bib.bib20);
[Ye et al. (2026)](#bib.bib5) further utilize this paradigm in settings
that incorporate additional signals, such as privileged information,
self-generated hints derived from environmental interactions, or
contextual guidance, with the goal of internalizing this external
knowledge into the model’s parameters.

While these works demonstrate the effectiveness of self-distillation,
they do not investigate when or why self-distillation may degrade
reasoning performance, especially in scenarios where a model must solve
problems entirely on its own, without interaction with the external
environment, which is the central question of our work.

#### Uncertainty Expression in LLM Reasoning.

[Kim et al. (2026)](#bib.bib6) introduce an information-theoretic
framework that identifies epistemic verbalization, the explicit
externalization of uncertainty, as informationally necessary for robust
reasoning. Our work answers a question this framework cannot readily
explain: *Under what conditions is this behavior encouraged or
suppressed? And if epistemic verbalization is necessary, why does
suppressing it lead to better performance in some domains, such as
Chemistry, while degrading performance in others?* We trace this to two
factors: conditioning context richness
(Section [3](#S3 "3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"))
and task coverage
(Section [6](#S6 "6 Relationship Between Task Coverage, Epistemic Verbalization and Generalization Ability ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")),
supported by a systematic analysis of recent on-policy self-distillation
methods across various models with varying pretrained capabilities.

#### Reasoning Compression.

Several recent methods aim to shorten reasoning traces while preserving
accuracy. GFPO ([Shrivastava et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)) filters training
rollouts by length and token efficiency within enlarged sample groups,
reducing GRPO’s length inflation by 46–85% on STEM and coding
benchmarks. OPSDC ([Sang et al., 2026](#bib.bib21)) uses a conciseness
instruction as privileged context, achieving 57–59% token reduction on
MATH-500. ConPress ([Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)) exploits
multi-question contextual pressure to elicit self-compressed traces,
yielding 30–60% reductions via SFT. Accordion-Thinking ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)) trains models to produce periodic step summaries that
can be discarded, achieving 3$`\times`$ throughput with a gap-vanishing
phenomenon during RL training. CEEH ([Luo et al., 2026](#bib.bib24))
proposes difficulty-aware entropy regularization to prevent entropy
collapse under length constraints.

Our analysis complements these efforts by showing that compression which
suppresses uncertainty expression, even when producing correct answers,
can harm OOD generalization, and that this effect is modulated by task
coverage. Therefore, the key challenge is to filter out non-informative
content while retaining epistemic expressions that enable iterative
belief refinement, rather than blindly compressing the reasoning
process.

## Appendix B Basis for Selecting Epistemic Tokens

To provide an empirical basis for our selection of epistemic tokens, we
analyzed uncertainty expressions across a diverse set of reasoning
models. We collected 9,600 reasoning traces from eight models spanning
four model families, including the Qwen3 family ([Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib11)) (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-32B), the
QwQ family ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)) (QwQ-32B), the
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen family ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)) (7B and
32B), and the OLMo family ([Olmo et al., 2025](#bib.bib12))
(OLMo-3-7B-Instruct).

The traces were generated on 600 math problems drawn from AIME
2024/2025, AMC 2023, and MATH500, with two samples per problem for each
model. Each reasoning trace was then provided to GPT-5 with the
following prompt:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This procedure yielded over 99,000
$`(\textit{span},\textit{trigger\_token})`$ pairs. We then ranked
trigger tokens by frequency within each model family (Qwen3, QwQ,
DeepSeek, and OLMo).

As shown in
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Basis for Selecting Epistemic Tokens ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
the ten markers maybe, wait, check, hmm, seems, perhaps, might,
actually, likely, and alternatively, together with their natural
variants, consistently appeared among the top-ranked uncertainty
expressions, supporting their inclusion across model families. While
several tokens, such as let me try/verify, I think, and make sure, were
excluded, our selected markers cover 75–93% of the occurrences of the
phrases in
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Basis for Selecting Epistemic Tokens ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").

|  |  |  |  |  |

| 2 | let me check (12.3%) | hmm (16.0%) | hmm (19.5%) | maybe (19.9%) |
| 3 | wait (12.1%) | wait (12.3%) | I think (13.0%) | wait (18.4%) |
| 4 | hmm (8.6%) | let me check (8.6%) | wait (10.6%) | likely (5.1%) |

Table 4: Top-15 uncertainty trigger tokens by frequency across model
families. Percentages indicate the proportion of extracted trigger-token
occurrences within each family.

Moreover, to account for uncertainty expressions not captured by our
token set, we conducted an independent LLM-as-a-Judge annotation
experiment
(Appendix [E.5](#A5.SS5 "E.5 Uncertainty Annotation via LLM-as-Judge ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"))
that captures the full range of uncertainty expressions. The resulting
distribution closely mirrors that obtained with our token-based
approach.

Finally, although the linguistic patterns used to express uncertainty
vary slightly across models, Qwen3, QwQ, and DeepSeek exhibit highly
similar distributions. OLMo also shares largely the same set of
uncertainty tokens, but differs in the relative frequency with which
individual tokens are used. The selected markers largely overlap with
expressions that human readers would naturally recognize as signals of
uncertainty, plausibly because these models are ultimately trained on
human-generated text.

## Appendix C Experimental Details

#### Training

For GRPO and SDPO training, we built upon the SDPO
implementation ([https://github.com/lasgroup/SDPO](https://github.com/lasgroup/SDPO))
and additionally incorporated the DAPO-Math-17k dataset. The original
DAPO-Math-17k dataset uses the following prompt format:

> Solve the following math problem step by step. The last line of your
> response should be of the form Answer: \$Answer (without quotes) where
> \$Answer is the answer to the problem.\n\n{question}\nRemember to put
> your answer on its own line after "Answer:".

We replaced this with a simpler format:

> {question}\nPlease reason step by step, and put your final answer
> within \boxed{}.

as we observed that this format consistently yielded higher evaluation
performance. For reward verification, we used the scoring function from
the verl framework, which extracts the answer from the \boxed{}
expression and verifies correctness via exact match followed by
mathematical equivalence checking using math-verify, adapted from
EleutherAI’s lm-evaluation-harness ([Gao et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)).

The GRPO and SDPO training hyperparameters are listed in Tables
[5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Training ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
[6](#A3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Training ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
and
[7](#A3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Training ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").
For the experiments on the relationship between task coverage and
learning performance in Figure
[9](#S6.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Training Logs ‣ 6.2 Relationship Between Task Coverage and Learning Performance ‣ 6 Relationship Between Task Coverage, Epistemic Verbalization and Generalization Ability ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
we reduced the question batch size to 64 due to the use of smaller
training questions.

## Appendix D More Ablation Study

### D.1 Effect of Maximum Response Length

In our main experiments, as detailed in Table
[5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Training ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
we set the maximum training response length to 20,480 tokens to avoid
prematurely truncating the long reasoning trajectories. Under a
budget-constrained setting, we additionally examine how the training
behavior of GRPO and SDPO changes when the maximum response length is
reduced to 4,096 tokens.

Figure 10: GRPO and SDPO with the maximum response length restricted to
4,096 tokens.

As shown in
Figure [10](#A4.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ D.1 Effect of Maximum Response Length ‣ Appendix D More Ablation Study ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
under the 4,096-token constraint, SDPO achieves relatively high training
scores early in training, whereas GRPO improves more gradually and
eventually reaches comparable training performance. More importantly,
GRPO consistently achieves higher performance on AIME24 and AMC23, while
SDPO plateaus at lower performance. Under a strict response budget,
SDPO’s tendency to produce shorter reasoning traces allows more
responses to be completed within the available token budget, which
likely contributes to its rapid initial gains. However, this early
advantage does not translate into continued improvement in reasoning
performance.

### D.2 Top-$`k`$ Distillation and Learning Rate

To examine the effect of various training hyperparameters on
self-distillation behavior, we conduct additional experiments by varying
the top-$`k`$ distillation parameter and the learning rate. As shown in
Figure [11a](#A4.F11.sf1 "In Figure 11 ‣ D.2 Top-𝑘 Distillation and Learning Rate ‣ Appendix D More Ablation Study ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
increasing top-$`k`$ from 100 to 256 yields no significant difference in
training dynamics or final performance. Meanwhile, as illustrated in
Figure [11b](#A4.F11.sf2 "In Figure 11 ‣ D.2 Top-𝑘 Distillation and Learning Rate ‣ Appendix D More Ablation Study ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
reducing the learning rate from $`1\mathrm{e}{-5}`$ to
$`1\mathrm{e}{-6}`$ slows the rate of degradation, but the model
ultimately converges to the same reasoning behavior.

a Effect of top-$`k`$ distillation ($`k=100`$ vs. $`k=256`$).

b Effect of learning rate ($`1\mathrm{e}{-5}`$ vs. $`1\mathrm{e}{-6}`$).

Figure 11: Ablation study on top-$`k`$ distillation and learning rate.
Both modifications fail to prevent the convergence toward degraded
reasoning behavior; a lower learning rate only delays the process.

[12](#A5.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ E.1 Per-Token Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
further extends this analysis by examining how the average per-response
count of each individual token changes under varying levels of
conditioning information. When examining the per-token counts, all
tokens exhibit a consistent trend:

\mathbb{E}\bigl[E(y)\bigr]\Big|_{(1)}>\mathbb{E}\bigl[E(y)\bigr]\Big|_{(3)}>\mathbb{E}\bigl[E(y)\bigr]\Big|_{(4)}>\mathbb{E}\bigl[E(y)\bigr]\Big|_{(2)},

where tokens such as wait, maybe, and perhaps are particularly

Figure 12: Per-token breakdown of epistemic token usage across the four

### E.2 Comparison of Epistemic Token Usage Across Models

Following the analysis of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B
(DeepSeek-Distill-7B) in
Section [3](#S3 "3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
we further compare epistemic token usage across three settings:
DeepSeek-Distill-7B, Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: ON), and Qwen3-8B
(Thinking Mode: OFF).

Figure 13: Comparison of epistemic token usage across
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen3-8B (thinking enabled), and Qwen3-8B
(thinking disabled).

As shown in
Figure [13](#A5.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ E.2 Comparison of Epistemic Token Usage Across Models ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
both DeepSeek-Distill-7B and Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: ON) produce
substantially more epistemic tokens than Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: OFF).
While the two thinking-enabled models share a similar tendency to
express uncertainty, they differ in their preferred epistemic tokens.
For instance, DeepSeek-Distill-7B frequently uses wait and employs
perhaps and maybe at comparable rates, whereas Qwen3-8B uses perhaps
relatively less and favors maybe. Qwen3-8B also uses alternatively and
check far more than DeepSeek-Distill-7B, and overall embeds a greater
amount of uncertainty within its reasoning.

Extending the discussion in
Section [3](#S3 "3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
we also observe that Qwen3-8B generates far fewer epistemic tokens under
solution-guided generation than under unguided generation. Across all
three settings, Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: ON) produces the most epistemic
tokens, followed by DeepSeek-Distill-7B, and then Qwen3-8B (Thinking
Mode: OFF).

(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Relationship Between Task Coverage and Learning Performance ‣ 6 Relationship Between Task Coverage, Epistemic Verbalization and Generalization Ability ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")),
we compare the change in epistemic token counts relative to the base
model on AIME24 across six training configurations: GRPO and SDPO, each
with $`|D|\in\{1,64,512\}`$.
Figure [14](#A5.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ E.3 Analysis of GRPO and SDPO Reasoning Patterns by Task Coverage ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
shows that GRPO tends to increase epistemic token usage relative to the

### E.4 Comparative Analysis of Epistemic and Overall Word Usage

In addition to analyzing epistemic tokens, we examine how the overall
word distribution in model responses shifts across the base model,
GRPO-trained model, and SDPO-trained model. We first extract English
words from each response using regular expressions and construct a
reference vocabulary $`\mathcal{V}`$ from all unique words appearing in
the base model responses. For each word $`w\in\mathcal{V}`$ and model
$`m\in\{\text{base},\text{GRPO},\text{SDPO}\}`$, we compute the average
per-response frequency:

|     |                                                       |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mu_{m}(w)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(w,r_{i}^{(m)}),
       ```                                                    |     | (6) |

where $`f(w,r)`$ denotes the number of occurrences of word $`w`$ in
response $`r`$. We then define the frequency shift
$`\Delta_{m}(w)=\mu_{m}(w)-\mu_{\text{base}}(w)`$ to capture how much
each word’s usage changes relative to the base model.

Using these frequency shifts, we compare the behavior of the predefined
set of epistemic tokens $`T`$ (as defined in
Section [3](#S3 "3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"))
against the rest of the vocabulary. Specifically, we compare
$`\{\Delta_{m}(w)\mid w\in T\}`$ against
$`\{\Delta_{m}(w)\mid w\in\mathcal{V}\setminus T\}`$ to determine
whether the changes in epistemic token usage are disproportionately
large relative to the overall shift in word distribution. This allows us
to distinguish whether the training procedure specifically amplifies
epistemic expressions or merely induces a uniform change across the
vocabulary.

Figure 15: Comparison of per-word frequency shifts ($`\Delta_{m}(w)`$)
for epistemic tokens ($`T`$) versus non-epistemic tokens
($`\mathcal{V}\setminus T`$) in GRPO- and SDPO-trained models relative
to the base model. Epistemic tokens exhibit disproportionately large
frequency changes compared to the general vocabulary, indicating that
the training procedures specifically amplify or suppress epistemic
expressions rather than inducing uniform changes across the word
distribution.

As shown in
Figure [15](#A5.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ E.4 Comparative Analysis of Epistemic and Overall Word Usage ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
the disparity between the two panels confirms that the observed
epistemic shifts are not byproducts of general vocabulary drift. Across
all model-method pairs, the average per-word shift over the full
vocabulary remains near zero ($`|\Delta|<1`$), whereas epistemic tokens
exhibit shifts up to $`30\times`$–$`40\times`$ larger in magnitude
(e.g., $`-11.9`$ and $`-12.2`$ for SDPO). This indicates that both
training objectives selectively target epistemic expressions rather than
uniformly perturbing the output distribution.

### E.5 Uncertainty Annotation via LLM-as-Judge

We employed epistemic markers as indicators of uncertainty expressions,
as they serve as practical and interpretable cues for regions where
uncertainty externalization is likely to occur. To more comprehensively
capture diverse forms of uncertainty expression, we additionally
leveraged GPT-5.4 ([Singh et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)) as an automated
annotator. Specifically, GPT-5.4 was prompted to identify and count
uncertainty expressions in each model-generated response. The prompt
used for this annotation is shown below.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

|  |  |
|----|----|
| Uncertainty Expression |  |
| “maybe there’s a simpler way” | “Wait, hold on. Is that correct?” |
| “I think the key here is to find $`s`$ and $`t`$ first, right?” | “I’m not entirely sure” |
| “perhaps there’s a relationship here” | “Hmm, that seems contradictory” |
| “perhaps I made a miscalculation” | “it seems a bit tricky” |
| “Wait, but this might get complicated” | “it seems less likely” |
| “maybe we can assume some symmetry” | “Alternatively, perhaps it’s better |
| “maybe we don’t consider $`n=0`$” | to think of it…” |
| “might not satisfy the surface area constraint” | “maybe I need another approach” |
| “actually, no. Let me think again.” |  |

Table 10: Representative examples of uncertainty expressions identified
by GPT-5.4. Expressions are drawn from model-generated reasoning traces
across all evaluated methods.

Table [10](#A5.T10 "Table 10 ‣ E.5 Uncertainty Annotation via LLM-as-Judge ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
presents representative examples of uncertainty expressions identified
by the annotator. The majority of identified expressions coincide with
the epistemic tokens examined in the previous analysis (e.g., maybe,
perhaps, wait), while others manifest as multi-token phrases such as
“I’m not entirely sure” that cannot be captured by single-token
frequency alone. This confirms that epistemic markers serve as a
reliable proxy for uncertainty externalization, while the LLM-as-Judge
approach provides complementary coverage over more diverse expression
forms.

|          |                 |
|----------|-----------------|
| Method   | Avg. Unc. Expr. |
| Baseline | 21.36           |
| GRPO     | 24.36           |
| SDPO     | 9.18            |

Table 11: Average number of uncertainty expressions per response, as

Figure 16: Box plot of uncertainty expression counts across methods.

Table [11](#A5.T11 "Table 11 ‣ E.5 Uncertainty Annotation via LLM-as-Judge ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
reports the average number of such expressions per response for each
method. When evaluated through LLM-as-Judge annotation, SDPO again
substantially reduces uncertainty expressions compared to both the
baseline and GRPO, consistent with the token-level analysis.
Figure [16](#A5.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ Table 11 ‣ E.5 Uncertainty Annotation via LLM-as-Judge ‣ Appendix E Additional Analysis of Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
complements this with a box plot comparison across methods: notably,
GRPO exhibits considerably greater variance than the baseline,
suggesting that RLVR can amplify inconsistency in hedging behavior. In
contrast, SDPO maintains consistently low counts with a narrow spread,
confirming that on-policy self-distillation suppresses unnecessary
hedging and self-doubt during reasoning.

## Appendix F Student–Teacher KL Divergence on Epistemic Tokens

We additionally measure the per-token KL divergence between the student
$`\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})`$ and the self-teacher
$`\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,c,y_{<t})`$ for each surface-form variant of
the epistemic tokens in $`\mathcal{T}`$. As shown in
Table [12](#A6.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix F Student–Teacher KL Divergence on Epistemic Tokens ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
every variant exceeds the corpus-wide mean KL of $`0.076`$, ranging from
$`1.9\times`$ (‘Wait’) to $`6.8\times`$ (‘ Hmm’). Notably,
sentence-initial variants (e.g., ‘ Hmm’ at $`6.8\times`$, ‘ wait’ at
$`3.8\times`$) tend to exhibit larger divergence than mid-sentence
forms, suggesting that the self-teacher most strongly disagrees at
positions where the student initiates epistemic deliberation. This
provides a quantitative explanation for the suppression of epistemic
verbalization under SDPO.

## Appendix G Analysis of Changes in Model Internal Uncertainty under Self-Distillation

To examine whether self-distillation also reduces the model’s internal
uncertainty, we further analyze token-level entropy as a measure of
internal uncertainty. Building on the analysis in
Section [3](#S3 "3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
we revisit the comparison between unguided and solution-guided
generation to assess whether access to richer information is associated
with lower predictive uncertainty.

|                             |          |                 |
|-----------------------------|----------|-----------------|
| Model                       | Unguided | Solution-guided |
| DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B | 0.385    | 0.218           |

Table 13: Token-level entropy under unguided and solution-guided
generation.

As shown in
Table [13](#A7.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Appendix G Analysis of Changes in Model Internal Uncertainty under Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"),
solution-guided generation reduces average token-level entropy by
approximately 43%, indicating substantially lower predictive uncertainty
when richer information is available. Moreover, under unguided
generation, epistemic tokens have an average entropy of 1.34,
approximately $`3.5\times`$ higher than the overall average, indicating
that epistemic verbalization tends to occur at positions of high
predictive uncertainty.

We next examine whether this lower-entropy generation behavior is
transferred to the student through self-distillation.

|-------------------------------|---------|-------|-------|
| Model                         | Initial | GRPO  | SDPO  |
| DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B   | 0.378   | 0.401 | 0.248 |
| Qwen3-8B (Thinking Mode: OFF) | 0.100   | 0.291 | 0.099 |

Table [14](#A7.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix G Analysis of Changes in Model Internal Uncertainty under Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
and
Figure [17](#A7.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ Appendix G Analysis of Changes in Model Internal Uncertainty under Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
show a consistent pattern in which GRPO increases token-level entropy
for both models, whereas SDPO reduces it, and this distinction persists
throughout training. These results indicate that the suppression of
uncertainty expressions through self-distillation is accompanied by a
genuine reduction in the model’s internal uncertainty.

## Appendix H Can Uncertainty-Encouraging Prompts Mitigate the Suppression?

We further investigate whether prompting the teacher to produce more
verbose reasoning with explicit expressions of uncertainty can mitigate
the performance degradation caused by the suppression of uncertainty
expressions. To this end, we design a modified regeneration prompt that
encourages detailed, step-by-step reasoning with uncertainty, and repeat
the reasoning behavior analysis (Section
[3](#S3 "3 LLM Reasoning Behavior Under Richer Information ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"))
and on-policy self-distillation experiments (Section
[5](#S5 "5 On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?"))
using this prompt.

[15](#A8.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Appendix H Can Uncertainty-Encouraging Prompts Mitigate the Suppression? ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
shows that the uncertainty-encouraging prompt partially recovers the
suppressed reasoning behavior: compared to the vanilla solution-guided
prompt, it produces longer responses (3,098 vs. 1,873 tokens) and more
epistemic expressions (31.4 vs. 8.8). However, both metrics remain far
below those of unguided generation, indicating that the presence of a
reference solution fundamentally constrains the model’s reasoning
verbosity regardless of the prompt instruction.

Figure
[18](#A8.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ Appendix H Can Uncertainty-Encouraging Prompts Mitigate the Suppression? ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
shows that the uncertainty-encouraging prompt leads to slightly higher
training scores and longer responses compared to the vanilla setting,
and this improvement carries over to AIME24 evaluation. Nevertheless,
both variants still suffer from substantial performance degradation,
suggesting that prompting alone is insufficient to resolve the
fundamental issue of uncertainty suppression in solution-guided
generation.

## Appendix I Comparison with OPSD from [Zhao et al. (2026)](#bib.bib3)

Recently, [Zhao et al. (2026)](#bib.bib3) proposed OPSD and demonstrated
performance gains in mathematical reasoning through on-policy
self-distillation, particularly on the Qwen3 series. Unlike our setup,
where both the student and the teacher either enable or disable thinking
mode, OPSD adopts a hybrid configuration in which the student operates
with thinking mode disabled while the teacher has it enabled.

As our experiments also confirm, enabling thinking mode produces
substantially longer responses with a greater number of epistemic
tokens, making this hybrid setup function more akin to conventional
teacher–student distillation, despite using the same underlying model.
We note that this configuration is inherently limited to model families
such as Qwen3 that support toggling thinking mode on and off.

For training efficiency, OPSD trains only on a response prefix (1,024
tokens by default), rather than the full student response. Unlike OPSD,
SDPO and our setup use full fine-tuning with verl ([Sheng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)), whereas OPSD adopts LoRA fine-tuning with trl ([von
Werra et al., 2020](#bib.bib18)) and a smaller batch size of 32 (vs. 256
in our setup), resulting in higher training efficiency but smaller
parameter updates per step.

a Hybrid vs. homogeneous setup performance over training.

b Response length and epistemic token usage in the homogeneous setup.

Figure 19: Training dynamics of OPSD hybrid distillation on Qwen3-1.7B
compared with our homogeneous chat-template setup. (a) In the hybrid
setup, the thinking-enabled teacher initially improves student
performance, but the gains diminish over time, whereas the homogeneous
setup shows a consistent decline. (b) Response length and epistemic
token usage under the homogeneous setup.

Under this hybrid setup with prefix learning in Qwen3-1.7B, as shown in
Figure
[19a](#A9.F19.sf1 "In Figure 19 ‣ Appendix I Comparison with OPSD from ( ) ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?")
(orange line), we observe an intriguing training dynamic. In the early
stages, the thinking-enabled teacher encourages the student to generate
longer responses while simultaneously improving performance,
highlighting the effectiveness of hybrid distillation during the initial
phase of training. However, as training progresses, performance steadily
deteriorates despite this early improvement. In contrast, under our
homogeneous setup, where both the student and teacher operate with
thinking mode enabled (pink line), performance declines consistently
throughout training. Response length and epistemic token count likewise
decrease steadily, consistent with our analysis.

While this hybrid distillation setup for the Qwen3 series presents an
interesting research direction with its own unique training dynamics,
such as why performance initially improves before declining and whether
this stems from changes in reasoning behavior or chat template mismatch,
a thorough investigation is beyond the scope of this work and is left
for future exploration.

our finding that self-distillation reduces uncertainty and makes outputs

performance, remains consistent across model sizes. Notably, the
performance degradation is more severe for the 1.7B model (45.9%)
compared to Qwen3-8B with Thinking Mode ON (12.1%) and
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (40.7%). This suggests that the
externalization of uncertainty may be particularly important for robust
reasoning in smaller models, which possess more limited inherent
capabilities.

## Appendix K Qualitative Analysis

### K.1 Unguided vs. Solution-Guided Generation

We analyze examples of $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{ug}}`$ (Unguided responses)
and $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{sg}}`$ (Solution-guided responses) introduced
in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Supervised Finetuning with Self-Distillation ‣ Why Does Self-Distillation (Sometimes) Degrade the Reasoning Capability of LLMs?").
Below, we present the two responses generated for the same problem. As
illustrated, the unguided response exhibits substantially more
uncertainty and exploratory reasoning, frequently revisiting
assumptions, considering alternative approaches, and self-correcting
along the way. In contrast, the solution-guided response proceeds in a
more concise and direct manner, arriving at each intermediate result
without detours.

Problem. How many ways can $`8`$ mutually non-attacking rooks be placed
on a $`9\times 9`$ chessboard so that all $`8`$ rooks are on squares of
the same color? (Two rooks are said to be attacking each other if they
are placed in the same row or column of the board.) Please reason step
by step, and put your final answer within $`\boxed{\phantom{0}}`$.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### K.2 GRPO vs. SDPO Generation

#### Problem (AIME24).

Find the number of ways to place a digit in each cell of a 2$`\times`$3
grid so that the sum of the two numbers formed by reading left to right
is 999, and the sum of the three numbers formed by reading top to bottom
is 99. The grid below is an example of such an arrangement because
$`8+991=999`$ and $`9+9+81=99`$:

|     |                                           |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \begin{array}[]{|c|c|c|}\hline\cr 0&0&8\\
       \hline\cr 9&9&1\\
       \hline\cr\end{array}
       ```                                        |     |

The correct answer is $`\boxed{45}`$.

GRPO explores with repeated reflections, deriving the extra constraint
$`a+b+c=8`$ beyond the pairwise sums, and correctly counts
$`\binom{10}{2}=45`$ solutions. SDPO proceeds directly and stops after
deriving $`a+d=b+e=c+f=9`$, multiplying $`10\times 10\times 10=1000`$
without checking the row-sum equation, thereby missing the additional
constraint $`a+b+c=8`$.
````
